The seasonal treat-based countdown might these days have expanded into cosmetics and booze, but nothing beats 24 days of chocolate. In our house, the arrival of the advent calendar was never simply a purchase; it was an event, placed ceremoniously on the mantelpiece and inspected with the seriousness usually reserved for fine art. The little cardboard doors promised not just sweets, but a structure to the darkening days of December, each one a tiny reassurance that winter could be sweetened, if only one square at a time.

***

That disclaimer, printed neatly at the top of the page, was the sort of thing Mara would normally skim past, but this year she found herself lingering over every word as she searched for the perfect calendar for her seven-year-old son, Eliot. She had intended to buy something practical, perhaps reusable, perhaps educational, but the moment she saw a calendar shaped like a snow-covered village, each window glowing with foil-wrapped chocolate, practicality gave up without a fight.

***

When it arrived, Eliot carried the box as if it contained treasure. On the first morning of December, before dawn had properly lifted, he padded into the kitchen in flannel pyjamas and carefully opened door number one. Behind it was a chocolate star, slightly misshapen, no bigger than a coin. He ate it with exaggerated concentration and announced that it tasted “like waiting for Christmas feels.” Mara laughed, then wrote the phrase down on the back of an envelope, unwilling to let it vanish with the morning steam from their tea.

***

As the month went on, the calendar became less an object and more a ritual. There were debates over whether the chocolate behind day nine was a reindeer or a dog, accusations that day 14’s treat was suspiciously smaller than day 13’s, and one near-crisis when Eliot briefly forgot to open a window and insisted the missed chocolate had to be saved forever. Outside, buses hissed through the rain and the afternoons darkened by four, but inside, those numbered doors offered a kind of cheerful order. Even Mara, who had long ago decided adulthood meant no longer needing such things, began to look forward to each day’s tiny reveal.

***

By Christmas Eve, the village on the front of the calendar was ragged with opened flaps, its magic nearly spent. Eliot held the final chocolate in his palm for a moment before eating it, as though understanding that finishing it meant the story was ending too. But Mara realised that was never really the point. The joy had not been in the size or quality of the chocolate, nor in whether the calendar was artisanal, nostalgic or on sale. It had been in the pause it created each morning — a small, sweet ceremony that made the month feel illuminated from within.
